outcome: Dickson's conjecture for finite families of linear forms with k ≥ 2 is still open in every source I could reach; since 26 January 2024 the movement is in weaker forms (at least two of k forms prime infinitely often, and bounded prime gaps), in special cases such as twin and Sophie Germain pairs, and in claimed proofs of Schinzel's Hypothesis H and of Bateman–Horn that include the linear case. Nearly all of that is conditional, unreviewed, or I could not read the primary text; the two AI-credited items that bear on Dickson at all (OpenAI's conditional DHL[40,2] of September 2026 and an Erdős #456 write-up built with ChatGPT-5.5-Pro that uses Dickson as a hypothesis) do not settle it.
problem_asks: The bullet asks, for each part: (1) Scope: every finite set of linear forms a_i + b_i·n, i = 1…k, with k ≥ 1 and each b_i ≥ 1 (the frozen wording says 'a finite set' of such forms, so the family is arbitrary, not one form). (2) Conclusion: there are infinitely many positive integers n for which all of the forms a_i + b_i·n are prime at the same time. (3) Exception clause: the conclusion is asserted only 'unless there is some congruence condition preventing it'. The frozen wording does not define that condition; the standard reading is admissibility (for every prime p, some residue class of n makes no form divisible by p). So the bullet asks for the simultaneous-primality conclusion for every admissible finite family, for every k. Special cases the statement contains, which are not separate asks but are cases of the bullet: k = 1 (Dirichlet's theorem, proved); the forms n and n+2 (twin primes); the forms n and 2n+1 (Sophie Germain pairs). Not asked by this bullet: the polynomial generalisation (Schinzel's Hypothesis H, Bunyakovsky) that the Wikipedia article mentions, which is a different statement with the forms replaced by polynomials.

events.what_happened: James Maynard, 'Small gaps between primes', arXiv:1311.4600, first posted 19 November 2013 (pre-window). The abstract (opened) states that for each k the prime k-tuples conjecture holds for a positive proportion of admissible k-tuples; unconditionally liminf (p_{n+1} − p_n) ≤ 600 and liminf (p_{n+m} − p_n) is finite for every m; under Elliott–Halberstam, liminf (p_{n+1} − p_n) ≤ 12. The abstract does not claim the full conjecture for any k ≥ 2.
events.revisions: v1 19 Nov 2013; v3 28 Oct 2019 (arXiv page). Journal version not checked in this run.
events.delivers: Unconditional, but only for a positive proportion of admissible k-tuples, per the abstract's own wording; plus the bounded-gap consequences. It gives no instance in which all forms of a given admissible family are prime infinitely often for any k ≥ 2.
events.remains: The full conclusion of Dickson's conjecture for every admissible family with k ≥ 2, and for any specific family. Also, the 'at least m of the forms' theorem for admissible k-tuples is attributed to Maynard and Tao by secondary sources; the fetched abstract does not state it.

checked_by.who: Polymath8 project (D. H. J. Polymath) and the group's refinements of Maynard's sieve
checked_by.qualification: Professional number theorists who refined the argument; the arXiv abstract of their paper cites Maynard's method and gives explicit H_m bounds for m = 2 to 5
checked_by.what_they_did: Refined Maynard's variational and sieve argument; their abstract reports H1 ≤ 246 unconditionally

events.direction: Partial. A weak Dickson-type statement (positive proportion of admissible k-tuples) and bounded gaps; it points the expected way but establishes no case of the full simultaneous-primality conclusion.

events.what_happened: James Maynard, 'Dense clusters of primes in subsets', arXiv:1405.2593, first submitted 11 May 2014 (v2 16 December 2014; pre-window). The abstract (opened) concerns intervals of length (log x)^ε containing many primes, and counts of strings of m congruent primes with p_{n+m} − p_n ≤ ε log x. The fetched abstract does not mention admissible k-tuples, a k_m threshold, Dickson's conjecture or the full prime k-tuples conjecture. A search snippet attributes an 'at least m primes' theorem for admissible tuples to Maynard and Tao and cites this paper, but that is not confirmed from the abstract.
events.delivers: Clusters of primes in well-distributed subsets; by the fetched abstract it does not concern the statement of Dickson's conjecture.
events.doubts: Relevance to the bullet depends on the admissible-tuple theorem that the abstract does not state; I have not verified that it is in this paper.
events.direction: Not about the conjecture as stated, on the abstract as read.

events.what_happened: D. H. J. Polymath, 'Variants of the Selberg sieve, and bounded intervals containing many primes' (Polymath8b), arXiv:1407.4897, first submitted 18 July 2014 (v4 22 December 2014; pre-window). The abstract (opened) says 'we can obtain the bound H1 ≤ 246 unconditionally', gives unconditional bounds on H_m for m ≥ 2 without numerical values for m ≥ 2 beyond stating they are explicit, and under the generalized Elliott–Halberstam conjecture gives H1 ≤ 6 and, for any admissible triple, infinitely many n with at least two of n+h1, n+h2, n+h3 prime. The abstract does not state an unconditional statement for admissible 50-tuples; secondary sources (Wu 2025 and a 2026 preprint seen in search) attribute that k = 50, m = 2 result to this project, which I did not confirm from the text.
events.delivers: Unconditionally: H1 ≤ 246 for consecutive prime gaps. Conditionally on the generalized Elliott–Halberstam conjecture: the weak Dickson statement for admissible triples (two of three forms prime infinitely often). Nothing unconditional about all forms prime.
events.remains: The full Dickson conclusion for every admissible family with k ≥ 2; the unconditional weak statement for k = 3 is not given here; the all-forms conclusion for any k ≥ 2.
events.direction: Partial: bounded gaps (unconditional) and a conditional weak Dickson for triples. Neither is the full conjecture.

events.what_happened: Itay Kaplan and Saharon Shelah, 'Decidability and classification of the theory of integers with primes', arXiv:1601.07099, first submitted 26 January 2016 (pre-window); published in the Journal of Symbolic Logic (2017, per a search result; the journal record was not opened). The abstract (opened) says: 'We show that under Dickson's conjecture about the distribution of primes in the natural numbers, the theory' Th(Z,+,1,0,Pr) is decidable, unstable and supersimple.
events.revisions: v1 26 Jan 2016; journal version 2017 per search result (not checked).
events.delivers: Conditional on Dickson's conjecture: a model-theoretic classification of the integers with a prime predicate. It uses Dickson as a hypothesis and establishes no case of it.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published (2017, per search result); referee reports not visible

events.direction: Conditional use of the conjecture; neutral on whether it holds.

events.what_happened: Idriss Olivier Bado, 'Dickson Conjecture Proof', a preprint in the AfricArXiv repository (DOI 10.31730/osf.io/ynxaf; listed under 'Preprint'), issue date November 2019 per a search snippet of the repository record (pre-window). The repository abstract (opened) says: 'based on the idea in [8] a partial proof of Dickson's Conjecture is provided'; it notes that Dickson stated it in 1904 and Schinzel and Sierpiński generalised it in 1958. A companion preprint by Bado and Tiemoko Gondo Patrick (October 2019, per a search snippet, not opened) says its work 'does not solve the dickson conjecture' but treats a related problem about primes p with ap + b prime.
events.delivers: Claims a partial proof of Dickson's conjecture. The abstract does not say which families, which k, or what kind of partiality, so what is established cannot be read from it.
events.remains: Everything outside the unspecified partial result, which on the abstract is undetermined.
events.doubts: Self-posted to a repository with no visible refereeing; the abstract states a 'partial proof' without its scope; the full text was not reached (the repository page gives the abstract only); the author has posted other claimed proofs of well-known problems (Beal's conjecture and the Erdős distinct subset sums conjecture, per a search snippet of the author's index), which I have not checked; the companion item disclaims solving Dickson's conjecture.
events.direction: Claims partial progress toward the conjecture; scope undetermined.

events.what_happened: Alexei N. Skorobogatov and Efthymios Sofos, 'Schinzel Hypothesis on average and rational points', arXiv:2005.02998, first submitted 6 May 2020 (pre-window); Inventiones Mathematicae 231(2) (2023), pp. 673–739. The abstract (opened) says: 'We resolve Schinzel's Hypothesis (H) for 100% of polynomials of arbitrary degree.'
events.revisions: v1 6 May 2020; journal version Inventiones 2023 (journal reference on arXiv page).
events.delivers: For a density-one set of polynomial families, ordered by height, Schinzel's Hypothesis H holds. This is a statement about almost all families; it does not give the conclusion for any particular finite family. The abstract does not say whether degree-1 families (linear forms, that is Dickson's case) are included; the body was not read, so that is open.
events.remains: Dickson's conjecture for any specific finite family of linear forms, and the exceptional set of families is not described in the abstract.

checked_by.qualification: A leading journal in arithmetic geometry and number theory
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted for publication (2023; journal reference on the arXiv page)

events.doubts: The degree-1 coverage question above is unresolved. The result is an average statement, so it is not a resolution of any specific family.
events.direction: Supports the conjecture on average; no counterexample; not a resolution of any specific family.

events.what_happened: Sun-Kai Leung, 'Moments of primes in progressions to a large modulus', arXiv:2402.07941, submitted 8 February 2024 (v2 5 July 2025). The abstract (opened) says: 'Assuming a uniform q-variant of the prime k-tuple conjecture', the paper computes moments of the number of primes in arithmetic progressions to a large modulus q, with Gaussian or Poisson behaviour and an exponential law for the least prime in a progression.
events.delivers: Conditional on a uniform q-variant of the prime k-tuple conjecture; distributional statements about prime counts in progressions. It does not establish any instance of Dickson's conjecture.
events.direction: Conditional use of a prime k-tuple hypothesis; neutral on whether Dickson holds.

events.what_happened: Carol Wu, 'On smooth gaps between primes using the Maynard-Tao sieve', arXiv:2403.19696, first posted 20 March 2024 (v2 17 April 2024; v3 13 October 2024). Published in INTEGERS 25 (2025), per a search result giving received 27 Oct 2024, accepted 14 Apr 2025, published 28 May 2025 (journal PDF not opened). The arXiv abstract (opened) says that Balog–Brüdern–Wooley's smooth-gap bounds are lowered to 47 by the Zhang, Maynard and Polymath8b advances, and that there are infinitely many m-tuples of primes whose gaps are all y_m-smooth. The k_m table (k_2 = 50, k_3 = 35265, k_4 = 1624545, k_5 = 73807570, k_6 = 3340375663) comes from a search-result extract of the Integers PDF, not from the fetched abstract.
events.revisions: v1 20 Mar 2024; v2 17 Apr 2024; v3 13 Oct 2024 (arXiv); INTEGERS 25 (2025) per search result.
events.delivers: Smoothness of gaps among tuples of primes, via the Maynard–Tao sieve. It concerns prime gaps, not the simultaneous primality of a fixed family. The k_m table reports the current thresholds for the weak 'at least m of k forms prime' form; per the extract it reports known values and does not lower them, which I did not verify.

checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted April 2025 and published May 2025 (per search result)

events.direction: Not directed at Dickson; reports weak-form thresholds without changing them.

The abstract (opened) states that the prime k-tuples conjecture holds for a positive proportion of admissible k-tuples, for each k, unconditionally, refining Goldston–Pintz–Yıldırım and Maynard. The wording matches Maynard's 2013 abstract.

checked_by.qualification: Journal of record for this article; refereeing standard not checked

events.direction: Restates a positive-proportion result; neutral on the full conjecture.

events.what_happened: Fred B. Holt, 'Eratosthenes sieve supports the k-tuple conjecture', arXiv:2502.20470, v1 27 February 2025 (v2 29 April 2025; v3 8 July 2025). The abstract (opened) treats the sieve as a discrete dynamic system and says 'we show that every admissible instance of every admissible constellation of gaps arises and persists in Eratosthenes sieve', and that population counts are consistent with the Hardy–Littlewood estimates of 1923. The abstract does not claim to prove the k-tuple conjecture.
events.revisions: v1 27 Feb 2025; v2 29 Apr 2025; v3 8 Jul 2025 (arXiv page).
events.delivers: Structural claims about the sieve and consistency with the 1923 estimates. By the abstract, no proof; evidence only.
events.doubts: The claims are structural and heuristic, and the abstract gives no numbers; the 'every admissible instance arises and persists' statement is a strong combinatorial claim I did not check. A search returned an AI-generated literature review of this paper, which I did not rely on. The later_work_cites_it value is true only as a self-citation: the 2026 Holt paper is by the same author.
events.direction: Heuristic support for the k-tuple conjecture; no case proved.

events.what_happened: Angelot Behajaina, Pierre Dèbes and Joachim König, 'Integrally Hilbertian rings and the polynomial Schinzel hypothesis', arXiv:2502.09959, v1 14 February 2025 (v2 8 April 2026). The abstract (opened) says the paper proves 'a polynomial variant of the Schinzel Hypothesis on prime values of polynomials with integer coefficients', conditional on the base ring being integrally Hilbertian; in the ring setting 'prime' is replaced by 'irreducible'.
events.delivers: A polynomial variant of Schinzel's Hypothesis in which the primes are replaced by irreducible elements of an integrally Hilbertian ring, conditional on that hypothesis for the base ring. It does not state the integer simultaneous-primality conclusion for linear forms.
events.direction: An analogue (irreducibility over a ring in place of primality over the integers); not the bullet's question.

events.what_happened: Ayla Gafni and Terence Tao, 'Rough numbers between consecutive primes', arXiv:2508.06463, v1 8 August 2025; no later version listed. The abstract (opened) says that almost all prime gaps contain a number whose least prime factor is at least the gap length, confirming a prediction of Erdős; the number of exceptional gaps with starting prime in [X, 2X] is O(X/log²X); and, 'assuming a form of the Hardy–Littlewood prime tuples conjecture', an asymptotic cX/log²X with c believed to lie between 2.7 and 2.8. erdosproblems.com marks Erdős Problem 682 as 'solved in the affirmative' by Gafni and Tao and mentions Dickson's conjecture only in the background, where Erdős's conditional counterexample uses 2183 + 30030d and 2201 + 30030d.
events.revisions: v1 8 Aug 2025; no later version listed (arXiv page).
events.delivers: Resolves Erdős Problem 682 (about gaps between consecutive primes and least prime factors). It does not settle any part of Dickson's conjecture. It uses a form of the prime tuples conjecture as a hypothesis for its sharper asymptotic.
events.direction: A different question. Dickson's conjecture appears only as background to a conditional counterexample; the result neither confirms nor refutes it.

events.what_happened: Huan Xiao (School of Artificial Intelligence, Zhuhai City Polytechnic, per a search snippet), 'From Golomb to Schinzel', Preprints.org, DOI 10.20944/preprints202505.0651.v2. A search snippet dates v2 to June 2025 (another snippet says posted 9 June 2025). The abstract, as seen in a snippet and not opened (preprints.org returned 403), says the Schinzel hypothesis, a conjecture on prime values of polynomials stated as Conjecture 1.1, is proved by Golomb's method. The snippets describe Conjecture 1.1 as the statement that infinitely many integers make a given set of irreducible polynomials simultaneously prime.
events.revisions: v2 June 2025 (search snippet). The May 2025 date for v1 is inferred from the DOI manuscript prefix 202505 and is not confirmed from a page I could open.
events.delivers: Claims a proof of Schinzel's Hypothesis H. Dickson's conjecture is the linear-form case of Schinzel's Hypothesis, so a valid proof would settle this bullet. Its validity is not checked.
events.remains: If the proof is valid, nothing remains for linear forms. Otherwise all of problem_asks.
events.doubts: Non-peer-reviewed preprint. I found no commentary or verification (search). The same author posted follow-ups claiming Bateman–Horn and Chowla by the same method (search snippets), which are themselves unverified. A claimed proof of a conjecture open since 1958 with no visible uptake. Full text not reached.
events.direction: Claims a proof of the statement that contains Dickson's conjecture, so it cuts toward the conjecture being true if valid.

events.what_happened: Huan Xiao, 'From Golomb to Bateman-Horn', Preprints.org, DOI 10.20944/preprints202512.2666.v1, posted 31 December 2025 (per a search snippet; not opened). The snippet says the same method is applied to the Bateman–Horn conjecture and 'We prove it by Golomb's method'.
events.delivers: Claims a proof of the Bateman–Horn conjecture. My reading, not from a source: the Bateman–Horn asymptotic for linear polynomials is the Hardy–Littlewood form of Dickson's statement, so a valid proof would give Dickson's conclusion for linear forms. Validity not checked.
events.remains: If valid, nothing remains for linear forms; otherwise all of problem_asks.
events.doubts: Unreviewed; the same method is claimed for Schinzel's Hypothesis and Chowla (search snippets); no verification found; full text not reached.
events.direction: Claims a proof of a statement that contains Dickson's conjecture, so it cuts toward truth if valid.

events.what_happened: DavidTurturean, forum write-up on erdosproblems.com Problem 456 (first post 4 May 2026, 22:33, per the problem's forum page; a further write-up on thread 92 dated 20 May 2026). The write-up is a 71-page Overleaf manuscript (not opened). It claims unconditional answers to the first two questions of Problem 456 (about m_n, the least integer with n | φ(m_n), and p_n, the least prime ≡ 1 mod n) and a conditional answer to the third, 'assume Dickson's conjecture for the admissible triple of linear forms t, 2t+1, 8t+1'. The author says the proof was developed by an automated scaffold that 'iteratively queried ChatGPT-5.5-Pro across several hundred rounds', and that ChatGPT-5.5-Pro checked it; the author says they checked the final proof themselves.
events.revisions: Further write-ups on thread 92 (20 May 2026) and 393 (3 May 2026) by the same author, which concern other problems and are not recorded here.
events.delivers: Problem 456 (author's claim): a positive lower density of n with m_n = p_n, which would refute the 'almost all' assertions. Q3 (conditional): on Dickson's conjecture for the single triple t, 2t+1, 8t+1, infinitely many primes p for which p − 1 is the unique n with m_n = p. Dickson's conjecture is used as a hypothesis for one triple; the event says nothing about whether it holds.
events.remains: Dickson's conjecture entirely; for the bullet the event touches one admissible triple only, under assumption.
events.directly_checkable: The author says the Dickson-conditional construction is about two pages of elementary arithmetic (Section 3); I did not check it. The unconditional parts are not checkable by me.
events.doubts: Single author, proof produced by an AI scaffold, 71 pages, no human reviewer, no formalisation (a commenter asked on 27 July 2026 for a Lean formalisation and got no answer). The problem page says comments are not verified for correctness. A 7 October 2025 comment argues that the stated inequality for Problem 456 is reversed, and Bloom replied that it was a typo; the statement's revision history was not checked.
events.direction: Conditional: asserts the Problem 456 Q3 result given Dickson for one triple. It is a case of nothing in Dickson's own bullet.

events.what_happened: Axiom Math, 'Lean formalization of bounded gaps between primes' (project page and PrimeGapsLib repository), announced 17 August 2026 per news coverage in search results (the project page itself has no date). It is a Lean 4 formalization, built on Mathlib and Kontorovich and Tao's PrimeNumberTheoremAnd (an internal fork, per the README), of the Maynard-sieve and Polymath8b argument for H1 ≤ 246, assuming Bombieri–Vinogradov. The README lists three main results: 246 from Bombieri–Vinogradov, 600 from Bombieri–Vinogradov, and 246 from Bombieri–Vinogradov plus an existence-of-certificate assumption. The project page says: 'It produced machine-checkable Lean 4 proofs built on Mathlib and Kontorovich and Tao's PrimeNumberTheoremAnd.' The page says human contributors then reviewed the code and organised it into PrimeGapsLib. Contributors listed on the page include Ken Ono, Jesse Thorner, Kenny Lau and Ashvin A. Swaminathan.
events.revisions: Repository has 7 commits per the README page; no date shown.
events.delivers: A Lean formalization, conditional on Bombieri–Vinogradov (a theorem), of H1 ≤ 246, which is already human-proved (Polymath8b). It is a formalization of earlier mathematics, not a new bound, and it does not address Dickson's conjecture.

events.what_happened: Julia Stadlmann, 'Bounded gaps between primes', arXiv:2608.31126, submitted 31 August 2026 (single version). The abstract (opened) says that Polymath8b proved H1 ≤ 246 and that 'the improved bound H1 ≤ 240' is obtained by combining Bombieri–Vinogradov with newer equidistribution estimates for smooth moduli. The abstract states no conditional hypothesis and does not mention admissible tuples. A search snippet says the argument uses an admissible 49-tuple; that is not in the abstract.
events.delivers: Unconditional bound H1 ≤ 240 on consecutive prime gaps. It is a bounded-gap result. Per a search snippet, its tuple has 49 shifts, i.e. a weak Dickson statement for one tuple size; that is not confirmed from the abstract.
events.doubts: Single author, very recent, no review found; later preprints build on it (see below) without an independent check.
events.direction: Bounded-gap improvement; neutral on the full conjecture; a weak-form input to later preprints.

events.what_happened: OpenAI, 'Improved Short Gaps Between Primes' (PDF on cdn.openai.com; dated 30 August 2026 per two tracker records; announced 3 September 2026 on X by Weijie Su per an aggregator). It claims liminf (p_{n+1} − p_n) ≤ 186, by proving DHL[40,2]: every admissible set of 40 integer shifts has infinitely many translates containing at least two primes. The companion repository (github.com/openai/PrimeGaps186; Lean namespace PrimeGap186) derives DHL[40,2] from three named inputs and applies it to an included admissible 40-tuple of diameter 186. The README says the inputs are 'established in the cited literature, but remain unproved inputs in this Lean development': kloosterman3_bound (a normalised three-variable Kloosterman bound of 3, attributed to Deligne via Katz 1988); kloosterman2_correlation_bound (a bound of 8p√p, attributed to Fouvry, Kowalski and Michel); and physical_integral_bounds (104 outer and 45 inner integral bounds plus three cap bounds). A Python-FLINT certificate (prime_gap_186_certificate.py) recomputes the numerical trials; the README says it does not discharge the inputs. The PDF was binary to my fetch and its text was not reached, so the paper's own sentence on the model's role is not quoted here.
events.delivers: Conditional on the three named inputs: (a) DHL[40,2], the weak Dickson statement for admissible 40-tuples with two primes required; (b) liminf (p_{n+1} − p_n) ≤ 186. Nothing unconditional in what I could read. The DHL[40,2] statement is a weaker form of Dickson's conjecture (at least two of 40 forms rather than all of them).
events.remains: The full conjecture: all forms prime simultaneously, for every admissible family and every k. The twin-prime gap of two remains open per the tracker. DHL[k,m] for other k or m is not claimed.

machine_checked.system: Lean (lake build; Comparator; Nanoda; Lean kernel), per the README

events.directly_checkable: The numerical certificate prime_gap_186_certificate.py and the Lean build (lake build PrimeGaps186), both described in the README. I did not run them.
events.doubts: (1) Unreviewed preprint; one tracker records 'Peer reviewed: No' and 'no independent human semantic review was located'. (2) The derivation is sorry-free but relies on three axioms that the README says are unproved in Lean: a Deligne-derived Kloosterman bound, a Fouvry–Kowalski–Michel correlation bound, and 104 + 45 + 3 numerical integral and cap bounds. The certificate does not discharge them. (3) Public X commentary was split on whether the 'conditional' status overstates the claim (per aggregator). (4) Levent Alpöge, per an aggregator, noted an earlier formalization at 188 and suggested 186 might be a coincidence. A third-party post credits the 188 work to 'Jack Kleeman and Claude'; I did not verify that, and it concerns 188, not this result. (5) Model naming differs across sources: 'GPT-6 Astra' (tracker, X post), 'GPT 6 Astra' (search summary).
events.direction: Cuts toward Dickson only in its weak DHL[40,2] form, and only conditionally; otherwise a bounded-gap bound.
events.object: An explicit admissible set of 40 integer shifts with diameter 186 (included in the repository). For this set, DHL[40,2] gives infinitely many n with at least two of n + h_i prime, conditional on the three inputs, which yields liminf (p_{n+1} − p_n) ≤ 186. The n are not explicit.

events.what_happened: Axiom Math announced a bound H1 ≤ 212 (a claimed improvement from Stadlmann's 240), per an aggregator page dated 3 September 2026. Ashvin Swaminathan posted the claim on X; Carina Hong, Alberto Alfarano, François Charton and Scott Kominers amplified it (aggregator). Swaminathan is quoted as saying: 'our result was formally verified by AxiomProver, relative to the existing literature.' Charton describes a 'human-AI collaboration' using 'substantial compute' (aggregator). No primary paper was found: the cited PDF (primegaps.axiommath.ai/bgp212.pdf) returned binary content in my fetch and the bgp212 page returned 404, and no arXiv listing was found.
events.delivers: A claimed bounded-gap bound of 212. Unverified. Not Dickson's conjecture.
events.doubts: No primary source reached. The author list (including Charton, Hong, Lau, Ono and Thorner) appears only in search summaries that cite the unreachable PDF, so it is unverified. 'Formally verified relative to the existing literature' does not say what the Lean check covers. Whether AxiomProver supplied any mathematics, as against verification, is not established by anything I read.
events.direction: Claims a bounded-gap improvement; neutral on Dickson's full conjecture.
people: François Charton (as credited in the aggregator)

events.what_happened: Fred B. Holt, 'On nonconvex constellations among primes I', arXiv:2603.25896, v1 26 March 2026 (v2 30 March 2026; v3 19 April 2026). The abstract (opened) says the author applies the methods to 'the Engelsma counterexamples (narrow constellations) of length J = 459 and span |s| = 3242', and that 'calculations show that none of the (459, 3242)-counterexamples occur before 9.7 E73'. The abstract does not define the property the 'counterexamples' violate.
events.revisions: v1 26 Mar 2026; v2 30 Mar 2026; v3 19 Apr 2026 (arXiv page; the page's version note says 9 April).
events.delivers: A computational bound on the first occurrence of certain narrow admissible constellations. By the abstract, not a proof of any case of the k-tuple conjecture.
events.doubts: Numerical. The abstract does not say what the 'counterexamples' are counterexamples to, so I cannot tell whether they bear on Dickson's conjecture. The version note (9 April) does not match the v3 date (19 April).
events.direction: Computational; not shown by the abstract to bear on Dickson's conjecture.
events.object: Per the abstract: narrow admissible constellations of length 459 and span 3242 (the Engelsma family). Calculations find none of the (459, 3242) counterexamples below 9.7 × 10^73. The abstract does not say these are counterexamples to Dickson's conjecture.

events.what_happened: Wayne Lewis (University of Hawai'i, Honolulu Community College), talk 'Infinitude of Sophie Germain Primes', 'Ultraproducts in Number Theory' seminar, 19 December 2025 (listing opened). The abstract says: 'We describe the details of an ultraproduct proof that there are infinitely many Sophie Germain primes.' The method is a nonprincipal ultrafilter built from complements of prime sets of cyclotomic polynomials, a Henselian valued field, a Bézout domain, and Łoś's theorem. No preprint is given and I found no arXiv posting.
events.delivers: If valid, the two-form case of Dickson's conjecture for n and 2n + 1 (infinitely many n with both prime). A single case, not the full conjecture.
events.remains: Every other family of linear forms, including the full conjecture.
events.doubts: Seminar abstract only; no written argument found. The abstract asserts that v = (s − 1)/2 is irreducible in its domain without showing it in the abstract. No engagement found in search.
events.direction: Claims a single case (Sophie Germain pairs), so it would cut toward the conjecture if valid.

events.what_happened: Taha Muhammad (ORCID 0000-0002-8954-9264), 'Twin Prime Conjecture (American Way)', Cambridge Open Engage working paper, version 1 posted 28 June 2026 (page opened). It claims 'the set of twin primes is asserted to be infinite', through 'Taha's Detector Prime Number' (TDPN), a criterion built on factorial expressions. The page says it has not been peer-reviewed by Cambridge University Press and does not mention AI or software.
events.revisions: Version 1 only as shown on the page.
events.delivers: Claims the k = 2 case of Dickson's conjecture: infinitely many n with n and n + 2 both prime. Only the twin case; no other family.
events.remains: The twin case itself, if the argument fails; every other family and the full conjecture.
events.doubts: One visible reader comment (Peter M, 28 June 2026) says the argument is not a proof and assumes, without showing, that a pair (p2, q2) exists. The method (TDPN) appears in no other source I found.
events.direction: Claims the twin-prime case, which would cut toward the conjecture if valid; the visible comment disputes validity.

disputes.summary: An aggregator page on the Axiom 212 claim says a 'Kintali' separately claimed H1 ≤ 236 with AI assistance and linked a paper on a homepage. The only 236 paper I found is Song and Yue (IACR ePrint 2026/1893), which has no AI statement. No Kintali paper was found in any search. Unresolved.

Two AI-credited bounds differ. OpenAI's 'Improved Short Gaps' gives liminf ≤ 186 (dated 30 August 2026), while the UCLA listing 'Prime gaps at most 182' (dated 4 September 2026, not opened) is credited to GPT-6 Astra as well. No source I read explains the difference.

Mor and Gupta (Baghdad Science Journal, 2024) present as their result a positive-proportion statement for admissible k-tuples whose abstract wording matches Maynard's 2013 abstract. Whether the full article adds anything is not established.

The model is named 'GPT-6 Astra' in the tracker and X post, 'GPT 6 Astra' in a search summary, and 'GPT-5.6 Sol' in a separate item on large prime gaps. Only the first two refer to the bounded-gap papers; the record uses the tracker's spelling.

summary: Since 26 January 2024 nothing in the sources I could reach settles Dickson's conjecture for any finite family of linear forms with k ≥ 2, and no peer-accepted result does so. The movement is in four places. (a) Weak Dickson (Maynard–Tao): at least two of k forms prime infinitely often. OpenAI's 'Improved Short Gaps Between Primes' (dated 30 Aug 2026, announced 3 Sep 2026, credited to GPT-6 Astra) proves DHL[40,2] and deduces liminf ≤ 186; the derivation is sorry-free Lean but rests on three named inputs that the README says are unproved in Lean, and it is unreviewed. (b) Bounded gaps: Stadlmann's H1 ≤ 240 (31 Aug 2026, unconditional, arXiv), a Song–Yue H1 ≤ 236 (IACR ePrint 2026/1893, 4 Sep 2026, no AI statement), an Axiom Math claim of 212 (3 Sep 2026, announced only, AxiomProver credited with formal verification), and Sharifi's listing of 182 (credited to GPT-6 Astra; not opened). These are not the bullet's question, though they sit on the same weak-form machinery. (c) Special and general cases: Lewis's Sophie Germain ultraproduct talk (Dec 2025), Taha's twin-prime claim (June 2026; a visible reader comment disputes it), and Huan Xiao's Preprints.org claims of proofs of Schinzel's Hypothesis (2025; the linear case is Dickson) and Bateman–Horn (Dec 2025; for linear polynomials it contains Dickson's asymptotic). I could not open Xiao's texts (403) and read them only as search snippets; if either were valid it would settle the bullet, so they are the decisive open items and carry no review at all. (d) Problem 456 (DavidTurturean, May 2026): an author-run write-up with a 71-page manuscript, produced by an automated scaffold that 'iteratively queried ChatGPT-5.5-Pro across several hundred rounds'. It uses Dickson's conjecture as a hypothesis for the single triple t, 2t+1, 8t+1 and proves nothing about Dickson. Gafni and Tao (Aug 2025) resolve Erdős 682, which uses Dickson only as background; that is a different question. Pre-window background: Maynard 2013 (a positive proportion of admissible k-tuples, unconditional), Polymath8b 2014 (H1 ≤ 246 unconditional; weak Dickson for triples under GEH), Skorobogatov–Sofos 2020/2023 (Schinzel H for 100% of polynomial families by height, which is a density statement and does not cover any given family), Kaplan–Shelah 2016 (conditional on Dickson), and Bado 2019 (a self-described 'partial proof' in a repository with no stated scope and no review). Close calls: (1) whether the weak DHL[k,m] statements count as moving a quantity the bullet names; I record them as weaker forms, since Dickson asks for all forms, not m of them. (2) Whether Skorobogatov–Sofos covers degree-1 families; the abstract does not say and I did not read the body. (3) Whether the AI attributions are load-bearing: for the OpenAI paper the attribution rests on trackers and an X post because the paper text was unreadable to me; for Axiom 212 it rests on a verification statement and a 'human-AI collaboration' description, with nothing read showing AxiomProver supplied mathematics. (4) Whether the Bateman–Horn and Schinzel claims bind Dickson; my reading is that they do, because the linear case of each is the Dickson statement, but that reading is mine, not the sources'. One minor point for §7.1 rather than research: the Wikipedia article as fetched gives the year as 1903, while search results give 1904.
competing_reading: The strongest case for a different reading: the 2025–2026 bounded-gap and weak-Dickson results are the only work since 2024 that moves a quantity close to the k-tuple machinery, namely the number of primes guaranteed among admissible k-tuples and the threshold k_m. A reader who counts 'the number of forms guaranteed prime' as the quantity the bullet names would record the 2026 DHL[40,2] result as progress, and the AI attribution would then be load-bearing. The opposite strong reading: the Xiao claims, if valid, settle the whole bullet, since Dickson is the linear case of Schinzel's H and of Bateman–Horn, so the status turns entirely on preprints nobody has reviewed and I could not open. A third reading treats the Lewis and Taha claims as single cases that count as events under §2.1 even though they are unreviewed and their steps look doubtful.
what_would_settle_it: (a) The full text of OpenAI's 'Improved Short Gaps Between Primes' PDF: the authors' own sentence on GPT-6 Astra's role, the exact DHL statement, and the list of inputs. (b) The Xiao preprints (2025-05 and 2025-12-31) read in full, and whether they cover linear forms, plus any referee or expert report. (c) The body of Skorobogatov–Sofos (arXiv:2005.02998), to see whether degree-1 families are covered and what the exceptional set is. (d) Any expert verification or refutation of the Lewis ultraproduct argument and the Taha twin-prime argument. (e) The Axiom 212 paper, if one exists, and the Sharifi 182 manuscript, to resolve the 182/186 discrepancy. (f) The Turturean manuscript's Section 3 and any human check of the Dickson-conditional construction, which would only settle Problem 456, not Dickson.

judgement.why: The statement asks that all forms of every admissible family be prime simultaneously infinitely often. Weak-Dickson results (at least m of k forms prime, positive proportion of tuples, Schinzel on average) and bounded-gap bounds answer a weaker question rather than moving a quantity the statement names, so they are variant; this is the closest call, since a reader could treat DHL[k,2] as a bound, but the statement has no 'number of forms prime' parameter. Conditional uses of Dickson (Kaplan–Shelah, Leung, Turturean) and formalisations are none. The only events claiming the statement or a case of it (Xiao's Schinzel and Bateman–Horn proofs, Lewis on Sophie Germain, Taha on twin primes) each carry several F10 signals: landmark claims, no uptake, non-refereed venues or no written text, methods the problem resists, and for Taha a specific unanswered objection. AI roles: OpenAI 186 and Sharifi 182 credited as generated on announcement/listing quotes; AxiomProver's quote is verification only, so none; Turturean's AI-generated proof is of a different problem.
judgement.doubts: The OpenAI and Sharifi AI attributions rest on an aggregator-quoted X post and a search snippet, not the papers. Mor–Gupta has year-only 2024 precision. If DHL[k,m] were read as a bound on this statement, the OpenAI 186 event (GPT-6 Astra, generated) would become the top event; I rejected that reading.
